access-card.etymology: access + card. Access comes from Latin accedere (to approach) — ad- (toward) + cedere (to go); card traces back to Greek khartēs (papyrus). Together: a little card that lets you in.
access-card.note: access + card = a card that lets you in

air-conditioner.etymology: air + conditioner. Conditioner is condition (to bring into a certain state) + -er. Literally 'a thing that conditions the air' — not just cooling, but managing humidity too.
air-conditioner.note: air + conditioner (a thing that adjusts the air)

air-fryer.etymology: air + fryer. Fryer is fry + -er. Literally 'a fryer that uses hot air instead of oil' — the core idea is getting that crispy fried feel without oil.
air-fryer.note: air + fryer = frying with hot air

air-purifier.etymology: air + purifier. Purifier comes from Latin purificare (to make pure), from the root purus (pure). Together: a machine that makes the air pure.
air-purifier.note: air + purifier (a thing that cleans the air)

airplane.etymology: air + plane. Air comes from Greek aēr; plane from Latin planus (flat), extended to 'a flat thing that glides through the air'. The combination captures the shape of the wings.

airship.etymology: air + ship. Air comes from Greek aēr; ship from Old English scip. Literally 'a ship of the air' — when balloons and dirigibles appeared in the 19th century, people naturally pictured them as vessels sailing the sky.
airship.note: air + ship = a ship that sails the sky

aisle.etymology: From Old French ele (the side passage of a church), tracing back to Latin ala (wing). A church's side passages are like the building's 'wings', and the word later extended to the walkways between store shelves.

alarm-clock.etymology: alarm + clock. Alarm comes from Italian all'arme! ('to arms!'), originally a battlefield cry. So an alarm clock carries a hint of 'urgent summons' — time's up, get up now!
alarm-clock.note: alarm + clock = the clock that shouts at you

alley.etymology: From Old French alee (walking; a passage), from the verb aler (to go — modern French aller). So an alley is literally 'a place for walking': a narrow footway squeezed between rows of houses.

aluminum-foil.etymology: aluminum + foil. Foil comes from Old French fuelle (leaf), tracing back to Latin folium (leaf) — so foil is literally 'a metal leaf', paper-thin. Together: a thin leaf of aluminum.

ambulance.etymology: From French ambulance, from ambuler (to move about), tracing back to Latin ambulare (to walk). In the 19th century it meant a mobile medical unit that followed the troops, later narrowing to the vehicle. At its root, an ambulance is 'a walking hospital'.

apple-cider-vinegar.etymology: apple + cider + vinegar. Cider comes via Old French sidre, tracing back to Hebrew shēkār (strong drink); vinegar is French vin aigre (sour wine). Together: apple juice fermented until it turns sour.

armchair.etymology: arm + chair. Arm comes from Old English earm; chair from Old French chaiere (seat). Together: a chair with rests for your arms — built for settling in comfortably.
armchair.note: arm + chair = a chair with armrests

back-cushion.etymology: back + cushion. Cushion comes from Old French coissin, tracing back to Latin coxinum (a pad made for the hip). Together: a soft pad for your back to lean on.
back-cushion.note: back + cushion = a pad to lean on

bag.etymology: From Old Norse baggi (bundle, pack). One of the most basic Germanic words — the core feeling hasn't changed since ancient times: a soft container you can fill and carry.
bag.note: b-ag: the thing you carry stuff in

bakery-section.etymology: bakery + section. Bakery is bake + -ery (a place); section comes from Latin sectio (a cutting). Together: the part of the supermarket where the bread lives.

baking-powder.etymology: baking + powder. Bake comes from Old English bacan (to bake); powder from Old French poudre (fine dust). Together: the powder that makes dough rise when you bake.

baking-soda.etymology: baking + soda. Soda comes from Medieval Latin soda, possibly from Arabic suwwad (a sodium-rich plant). Together: the alkaline powder used in baking.

ballpoint-pen.etymology: ball + point + pen. Early fountain pens leaked, so in the 1930s the Hungarian László Bíró invented a pen with a tiny ball in its tip that rolls the ink out evenly — hence 'ball-point'.
ballpoint-pen.note: ball + point + pen = the rolling-ball pen

bank.etymology: From Italian banca (bench) — Renaissance Italian bankers handled money from benches in the marketplace, and the 'bench' became the name of the institution. When a business failed, the bench was smashed: banca rotta ('broken bench') gave us bankrupt.
bank.note: b-ank: the money place (also a river 'bank')

barcode.etymology: bar + code. Bar comes from Old French barre (rod); code from Latin codex (an ancient writing tablet). Together: a code made of stripes — the retail standard since the 1970s.

basil.etymology: From Greek basilikon (royal, kingly), from basileus (king). The ancient Greeks considered this herb noble and regal, and the name stuck — basil carries 'the herb of kings' in its roots.

basket.etymology: From Old French baschoe, possibly from a Celtic word for basket. The earliest baskets were woven from twigs and vines, so the core feeling is 'a soft container woven with gaps'.

bath-mat.etymology: bath + mat. Bath comes from Old English bæð, originally soaking and washing; mat from Latin matta, a woven straw pad. Together: the little pad you stand on at bath time.

bath-salts.etymology: bath + salts. Bath comes from Old English bæð (soaking); salts is the plural of salt, from Latin sal. Literally: the salt you toss into the tub.

bath-sponge.etymology: bath + sponge. Sponge comes from Greek spongos, originally the porous sea creature itself. Together: the sponge you wash with — absorbent and soft.

bath-towel.etymology: bath + towel. Towel comes via Old French toaille from Proto-Germanic thwahlijo, 'a cloth for wiping'. So a bath towel is the big cloth you dry off with.

bathrobe.etymology: bath + robe. Robe comes from Old French robe, originally 'plundered garments', later any loose long garment. Together: the long soft robe you wrap up in before and after a bath.

bathroom-cabinet.etymology: bathroom + cabinet. Cabinet comes from Old French cabinet, originally 'a little room', which shrank into 'a little cupboard'. Together: the small cupboard in the bathroom.

bathroom-cleaner.etymology: bathroom + cleaner. Cleaner is the verb clean + -er, 'a thing that makes clean'. Plainly: the cleaning product for the bathroom.

bathroom-door.etymology: bathroom + door. Door comes from Old English duru, one of the oldest Germanic words — it has always simply meant 'the way in and out'. Together: the door to the bathroom.

bathtub.etymology: bath + tub. Tub comes from Middle Dutch tubbe, a round wooden vessel. Together: the big tub you fill with water and soak in — a container you can lie down inside.

bay-leaf.etymology: bay + leaf. Bay comes via Old French baie from Latin bāca (berry) — the laurel tree bears berries, and the tree took its name from them; leaf comes from Old English lēaf. Together: the leaf of the laurel tree.

bed.etymology: From Old English bedd, tracing back to Proto-Germanic *badjam, possibly related to 'a dug-out hollow, a resting place'. The core feeling: the fixed spot where you lie down and rest.
bed.note: b-e-d looks like a bed with posts at both ends

bed-sheet.etymology: bed + sheet. Sheet comes from Old English scēte, originally 'a piece of cloth'. Together: the layer of cloth spread over the bed.

bedside-lamp.etymology: bedside + lamp. Bedside is bed + side; lamp comes from Greek lampas (torch). Together: the lamp that sits beside the bed.

bedspread.etymology: bed + spread. Spread comes from Old English sprǣdan (to stretch out, unfold). Together: the cover you spread across the bed — one big, flat layer over everything.
bedspread.note: bed + spread (the cover spread on top)

bench.etymology: From Old English benc, tracing back to Proto-Germanic *bankiz, 'a long seat'. It shares a root with bank — Renaissance Italian bankers did business from benches in the marketplace, and the 'bench' became the financial institution.

beverage-section.etymology: beverage + section. Beverage comes from Old French bevrage, from bevre (to drink), tracing back to Latin bibere (to drink). Together: the part of the store that sells things to drink.

bicycle.etymology: bi- + cycle. Bi- is Latin for 'two'; cycle comes from Greek kyklos (circle, wheel). Literally 'two wheels' — when the machine was invented in the 19th century, the name was as direct as it gets.

bike-lane.etymology: bike + lane. Bike is short for bicycle, from bi- (two) + cycle (wheel); lane comes from Old English lanu (narrow way). Together: the narrow strip reserved for bikes.

billboard.etymology: bill + board. Bill comes from Middle English bille (a written document); board from Old English bord (plank). Together: a big board for posting notices — originally just a wooden wall for pasting posters.

binder-clip.etymology: binder + clip. Bind comes from Old English bindan (to tie, to hold together), plus -er for 'a tool that binds'; clip comes from Old English clyppan (to embrace, grip tightly). Together: the clip that grips a stack of paper.

black-pepper.etymology: black + pepper. Pepper comes from Old English pipor, via Latin piper and Greek peperi, ultimately from Sanskrit pippali. The word's journey mirrors pepper's route from India to Europe along the spice roads.

black-vinegar.etymology: black + vinegar. Vinegar comes from French vin aigre, literally 'sour wine' (vin wine + aigre sour). Together: the dark, tangy seasoning.

blanket.etymology: From Old French blanchet ('little white cloth'), from blanc (white) — medieval wool blankets were mostly undyed and whitish, and the name stayed. The core feeling: a big, warm cover.

blender.etymology: The verb blend + -er: literally 'a machine that blends'. Blend comes from Old Norse blanda (to mix, stir together) — the core feeling is stirring different things into one.

blinds.etymology: The plural of blind used as a noun: 'a thing that blocks sight'. Blind comes from Old English blind (unable to see). It's plural because a window is covered by many slats — they keep you from seeing out and others from seeing in.

boat.etymology: From Old English bāt, tracing back to Proto-Germanic *baitaz. One of the oldest Germanic words — the core feeling is unchanged: a thing that floats and carries people.
boat.note: b-oat: the little vessel on the water

body-wash.etymology: body + wash. Body comes from Old English bodig, wash from Old English wæscan — both among the most basic Germanic words. Together: the liquid soap you wash your body with.

bonito-powder.etymology: bonito + powder. Bonito comes from Spanish — a diminutive of bueno (good), named for how tasty the fish is. Together: powder made from dried bonito.

bookshelf.etymology: book + shelf. Shelf comes from Middle Low German schelf, originally 'a flat ledge of rock'. Together: the flat board your books stand on.

bouillon-powder.etymology: bouillon + powder. Bouillon comes from French bouillir (to boil), so it's literally 'the broth you get by boiling'. Together: stock concentrated into a powder.

bowl.etymology: From Old English bolla, tracing back to Proto-Germanic *bullǭ, 'a round thing'. The core feeling of bowl has always been 'half a sphere' — a scooped-out round container.
bowl.note: b-owl: the round dish for soup and rice

bridge.etymology: From Old English brycg, tracing back to Proto-Germanic *brugjō, possibly related to 'tree trunk' — the oldest bridges were felled logs. The core feeling is primal: the one thing that carries you across.

brown-sugar.etymology: brown + sugar. Sugar comes via Old French sucre from Arabic sukkar and Sanskrit śarkarā. Together: sugar that keeps its molasses — not fully refined, so it stays brown.

bucket.etymology: From Old French buket ('a small water vessel'), possibly tracing back to Old English buc (jug). The core feeling: a round container with a handle you can carry.

bus.etymology: Short for omnibus, Latin for 'for everyone' (the dative plural of omnis, 'all'). In the 1820s a French public coach service called Voiture omnibus took off, and the Latin ending became the whole world's word for 'bus'.

bus-stop.etymology: bus + stop. Bus is short for omnibus, Latin for 'for everyone'; stop comes from Old English stoppian. Together: the place where the bus stops.

business-card.etymology: business + card. Business is busy + -ness, originally 'the state of being busy', later 'one's affairs, trade'. Together: the little card you hand over when you talk business.

cabinet.etymology: From Old French cabinet, originally 'a little room' (a diminutive of cabane, hut). It later shrank into 'a little cupboard', but the core image of 'a small enclosed space' remains.

cable-car.etymology: cable + car. Cable comes from Old French chable (thick rope); car from Latin carrum (wheeled vehicle). Together: a car pulled along by a steel cable — the mountain and gondola ride.
cable-car.note: cable + car = the car on a cable

cafe.etymology: From French café, via Turkish kahve, from Arabic qahwa. The word originally meant the drink itself — coffee — and in Europe it came to mean the shop that serves it.

calendar.etymology: From Latin kalendarium, originally 'an account book' — Romans settled their accounts on the first day of each month (the kalendae), so the book that tracked the days took that name. It later became 'the chart of dates'.

camper-van.etymology: camper + van. Camp comes from Latin campus (open field, battleground); van is short for caravan (the great trade-convoy wagon). Together: a van you can live and camp in.

can-opener.etymology: can + opener. Can comes from Old English canne (container); opener is open + -er. Together: the tool that opens cans — as direct as names get.

candle.etymology: From Old English candel, tracing back to Latin candela, from candere (to shine, to glow white-hot). The core feeling of candle has been tied to 'glowing white light' since its roots.

canned-food.etymology: canned (the adjective from can) + food. Can comes from Old English canne (container), now specifically a metal tin. Together: food preserved in a can — a technology invented in the 19th century for feeding armies.

canoe.etymology: From Spanish canoa, tracing back to canaoa in the Arawak language of the Caribbean. Columbus recorded the word on reaching the Americas, so canoe carries a piece of indigenous American watercraft history.

car.etymology: From Old French carre, tracing back to Latin carrum (the Celts' four-wheeled war chariot). So car has an ancient chariot hiding in its roots — it later meant any wheeled vehicle, then settled on the automobile.

cardamom.etymology: From Greek kardamōmon, possibly a blend of kardamon (cress) + amōmon (an Indian spice). Two ancient spices fused into one word — a trace of its journey from South Asia to Europe.

cashier.etymology: From French caissier: caisse (money chest) + -ier (person). Caisse traces back to Latin capsa (box). So a cashier is literally 'the keeper of the money box', and later the counter where the box sits.
cashier.note: cash + ier = the person who takes your money

ceiling-light.etymology: ceiling + light. Ceiling comes from Old English (to cover), tracing to Latin caelare (to carve or panel an interior); light from Old English lēoht. Together: the light mounted on the ceiling.

chair.etymology: From Old French chaiere, tracing back to Latin cathedra (seat — also the root of cathedral, the bishop's seat). Originally a dignified high-backed seat, it later democratized into any chair.

charger.etymology: The verb charge + -er. Charge comes from Old French chargier, tracing to Late Latin carricare (to load), from carrus (wagon). Originally 'to load a cart', later extended to 'loading energy into a battery'.

checkout-counter.etymology: checkout + counter. Check comes from Old French eschec (chess 'check!'), extended to 'verify'; counter from Latin computare (to reckon). Together: the counter where purchases are checked and totted up.

chicken-bouillon-powder.etymology: chicken + bouillon + powder. Bouillon is French for 'boiled broth'. Together: chicken stock concentrated into a powder — the umami staple of Asian kitchens.

chili-bean-paste.etymology: chili + bean + paste. Chili comes from Nahuatl chīlli (the Aztec language); paste from Late Latin pasta (a doughy mass). Together: a fermented paste of chilis and beans — the flavor base of Sichuan cooking.

chili-flakes.etymology: chili + flakes. Chili comes from Nahuatl chīlli; flake from Old Norse flak (thin slice). Together: dried chilis crushed into flakes.

chili-oil.etymology: chili + oil. Oil comes from Old French oile, tracing back to Latin oleum (olive oil) and Greek elaion. Together: oil steeped with chilis.

chili-powder.etymology: chili + powder. Chili comes from Nahuatl chīlli; powder from Old French poudre (fine dust). Together: chilis ground to a powder.

chili-sauce.etymology: chili + sauce. Sauce comes from Old French sauce, tracing back to Latin salsus (salted), from sal (salt). Sauce originally meant 'a salty seasoning liquid' — here, one made of chilis.

chopsticks.etymology: chop + sticks. In 17th-century pidgin English chop meant 'quick' (chop-chop = hurry up), so chopsticks is literally 'quick sticks' — how early European traders described the utensil.
chopsticks.note: Chopsticks is a plural noun — always ends in -s.

cilantro.etymology: From Spanish cilantro, tracing back to Latin coriandrum (the coriander plant). North America adopted the Spanish word for the leaves; the seeds go by coriander. So cilantro carries the flavor of the Spanish-speaking food world.

cinnamon.etymology: From Greek kinnamōmon, possibly from Malay or Hebrew qinnāmōn. This bark was a precious spice in antiquity, traveling the spice routes from Ceylon to the Mediterranean — its name carries traces of every language along the way.

cinnamon-bark.etymology: cinnamon + bark. Bark comes from Old Norse bǫrkr (tree bark). Together: the bark of the cinnamon tree, used whole or curled into sticks.

cleaner.etymology: The verb clean + the noun ending -er: literally 'a thing that makes things clean'. Clean comes from Old English clǣne, which meant both 'clean' and 'pure'.

cleaning-brush.etymology: cleaning + brush. Brush comes from Old French broisse, originally the twigs of brushwood — bundle the twigs and you have a brush. Plainly: the tool you scrub things clean with.

cleansing-oil.etymology: cleansing + oil. Cleanse comes from Old English clǣnsian — like clean, but with a stronger sense of purifying, of washing impurity away. Together: the oil you clean your face with.

clock.etymology: From Middle Dutch clocke, meaning 'bell'. The earliest mechanical clocks struck a bell to tell the hour, so the whole device took its name from the sound. At its core, a clock is still 'the ringer that announces the time'.

closet.etymology: From Old French closet (little room): clos (closed) + -et (the diminutive). Traces back to Latin claudere (to shut). The core feeling: a small space that closes.
closet.note: close + t: the shut-away space for clothes

cloth.etymology: From Old English clāth (woven fabric), tracing back to Proto-Germanic *klaithaz. As basic as words get: the source of the whole idea of 'cloth'.

clothes.etymology: The plural of cloth, from Old English clāth ('a piece of cloth'). Plural because an outfit is many pieces of fabric. The core feeling: the cloth you drape on your body.
clothes.note: Always plural; the general word for what you wear

cloves.etymology: The plural of clove, from Old French clou (nail) — the dried flower buds look like little nails. The word literally describes the spice's shape.

coach.etymology: From the Hungarian village of Kocs, where a comfortable spring-suspension carriage was invented in the 15th century. Coach literally means 'the wagon from Kocs' — later any long-distance vehicle, and even the person who carries you to your goal.
coach.note: Coach also means 'trainer'; the long-distance bus

coffee-machine.etymology: coffee + machine. Coffee comes from Arabic qahwa; machine from Latin machina (device). Together: the machine that makes coffee — same as coffee maker.

coffee-maker.etymology: coffee + maker. Coffee came via Turkish kahve from Arabic qahwa, originally the name of the drink. Plainly: the machine that brews coffee.

coffee-table.etymology: coffee + table. Coffee comes from Arabic qahwa; table from Latin tabula (board). Together: the low table your coffee cup sits on — a fixture of 20th-century living-room life.
coffee-table.note: coffee + table = the low living-room table

comb.etymology: From Old English camb, tracing all the way to Proto-Indo-European *gombh- (teeth). In its oldest sense a comb is 'a row of teeth' — a tool of neatly lined-up tines.
comb.note: The b in comb is silent.

computer.etymology: compute + -er. Compute comes from Latin computare: com- (together) + putare (to reckon). A computer originally meant 'a person who calculates' — only in the 20th century did the machine take the name.

conditioner.etymology: The verb condition (to bring into good condition) + -er. Condition comes from Latin condicio, originally 'agreement, terms', extended to 'bringing something into a certain state'. So conditioner is 'the thing that puts your hair in good condition'.

conference-table.etymology: conference + table. Conference comes from Latin conferre (to bring together): con- (together) + ferre (to carry). Together: the table everyone brings their opinions to.

construction-zone.etymology: construction + zone. Construction comes from Latin construere (to pile up, build); zone from Greek zōnē (belt, band). Together: the area where building is underway.

convenience-store.etymology: convenience + store. Convenience comes from Latin convenire (to come together, to suit): con- (together) + venire (to come); store from Old French estore (provisions). Together: a store that exists for convenience.

cooking-wine.etymology: cooking + wine. Wine comes from Old English wīn, tracing back to Latin vinum. Together: wine for the kitchen — for cutting fishiness and adding aroma, not for drinking.

coriander-seeds.etymology: coriander + seeds. Coriander comes from Greek koriannon, said to be named for a smell that reminded people of bedbugs (koris). Together: the seeds of the coriander plant — milder and more citrusy than the leaves.

corner.etymology: From Old French corniere (corner), tracing back to Latin cornu (horn, point). Hiding in corner is the image of an animal's horn — a sharp, jutting turn.

cornstarch.etymology: corn + starch. Corn originally meant 'grain' in British English; starch comes from Old English stercan (to stiffen) — because starch paste hardens as it dries. Together: starch extracted from corn.

cosmetics.etymology: From Greek kosmētikos, 'skilled at arranging and adorning', tracing up to kosmos (order; the universe). The core feeling is 'putting your appearance in beautiful order' — cosmetics bring order and beauty to the face.

cotton-ball.etymology: cotton + ball. Cotton entered European languages through Arabic qutn, the plant fiber itself. Together: cotton rolled into a little ball.

cotton-pad.etymology: cotton + pad. Pad comes from Low German pad, a small flat soft piece. Together: cotton pressed into a thin sheet — where the cotton ball is a sphere, the pad is a slice.

cotton-swab.etymology: cotton + swab. Swab comes from Middle Dutch zwabber, originally the mop sailors used on deck. Together: a little stick tipped with cotton at both ends.

coupon.etymology: From French coupon: couper (to cut) + -on, literally 'a piece cut off' — early coupons were clipped out of newspapers and catalogs. The word still carries that scissors-and-paper image.

crosswalk.etymology: cross + walk. Cross comes from Old English cros (cross, across); walk from Old English wealcan. Together: the walkway across the road — first just a painted line, later the bold zebra stripes.
crosswalk.note: cross + walk = where you cross the street

cruise-ship.etymology: cruise + ship. Cruise comes from Dutch kruisen (to cross back and forth, to sail to and fro); ship from Old English scip. Together: the great ship that sails around for pleasure — modern tourism's symbol of luxury.

cumin.etymology: From Latin cuminum, via Greek kyminon, ultimately probably Semitic (Hebrew kammōn). The spice has seasoned the Mediterranean for thousands of years, and its name traveled through just as many ancient languages.

cumin-powder.etymology: cumin + powder. Cumin comes from Latin cuminum; powder from Old French poudre. Together: cumin ground to a powder.

curry-powder.etymology: curry + powder. Curry comes from Tamil kaṟi (sauce; meat dish) — the British carried the word home from India and stretched it to cover all sorts of spice blends. Together: a powder of mixed Indian spices.

curry-roux.etymology: curry + roux. Roux is French for 'russet brown' — butter and flour cooked until they color become a sauce base. Japanese curry borrowed the French technique and pressed the spiced roux into blocks.

curtain.etymology: From Old French cortine, tracing back to Latin cortina (enclosing screen, curtain). In Roman times cortina also meant the theater curtain, so curtain has always carried the sense of 'hiding what's behind'.

curtains.etymology: The plural of curtain, from Old French cortine (Latin cortina, enclosing screen). Usually plural because they hang as a pair, one panel on each side of the window.

cushion.etymology: From Old French coissin, tracing back to Latin coxinum, from coxa (hip). So a cushion is, at its roots, 'a pad designed for your backside' — soft and supporting.

cutting-board.etymology: cutting + board. Cut comes from Middle English cutten; board from Old English bord (plank). Together: the board you cut things on.

dark-brown-sugar.etymology: dark + brown + sugar. Sugar comes from Arabic sukkar and Sanskrit śarkarā. Together: sugar that keeps even more molasses, darker in color and richer in flavor than regular brown sugar.

dark-soy-sauce.etymology: dark + soy sauce. Soy comes from Japanese shōyu, itself from the Chinese word for soy sauce. Together: soy sauce that's darker and thicker than the light kind — 老抽 in Cantonese cooking.

dehumidifier.etymology: de- (remove) + humid + -ify (make) + -er. Humid comes from Latin humidus (moist). Literally 'a machine that un-humidifies the air' — the exact opposite of a humidifier.
dehumidifier.note: de- (remove) + humid + ifier = the dryer of air

deli-section.etymology: Deli is short for delicatessen, from German Delikatessen (fine foods): délicat (delicate) + Essen (food). Together: the section that sells fine prepared foods.

dental-floss.etymology: dental + floss. Dental comes from Latin dens (tooth); floss from Old French flosche, originally the softest, fluffiest layer of silk. Together: fine thread for your teeth.

deodorant.etymology: Latin de- (remove) + odor (smell) + -ant (agent): literally 'the thing that removes smell'. As direct as it gets — it takes away the odor you don't want.

desk.etymology: From Medieval Latin desca, tracing back to Latin discus (disc, a broad flat board) — the same root as dish. Originally a slanted writing board, it later flattened into today's desk.

desk-lamp.etymology: desk + lamp. Desk comes from Medieval Latin desca, originally a slanted writing board; lamp from Greek lampas (torch). Together: the little work light on your desk.

diffuser.etymology: diffuse + -er. Diffuse comes from Latin diffundere (to pour out in all directions): dis- (apart) + fundere (to pour). So a diffuser's core feeling is 'pouring scent out in every direction'.

discount.etymology: From Medieval Latin discomputare: dis- (away) + computare (to count). Literally 'to count some off the total' — the price, with a piece taken off.
discount.note: dis- (off) + count = a piece counted off

dish-soap.etymology: dish + soap. Dish comes from Old English disc (plate), tracing back to Latin discus (disc); soap from Old English sāpe. Together: soap for the dishes.

dishwasher.etymology: dish + washer. Washer is wash + -er. Literally 'the machine that washes the dishes' — no ambiguity anywhere.

disinfectant.etymology: dis- (remove) + infect + -ant. Infect comes from Latin inficere, originally 'to dye, to taint'. So a disinfectant is literally 'the thing that removes the taint' — it kills the dirt you can't see.

display-cabinet.etymology: display + cabinet. Display comes from Old French desploiier (to unfold, spread out): dis- (apart) + plicare (to fold). Together: the cabinet that spreads things out for people to see.

document.etymology: From Latin documentum, from docere (to teach). A document was originally 'a thing that teaches or serves as proof' — it still carries that feeling of 'something with authority, something you can cite'.

door.etymology: From Old English duru, one of the oldest Germanic words. Its Proto-Indo-European root *dhwer- means 'doorway' across many languages. The core feeling: the opening that opens and closes.

doorbell.etymology: door + bell. Door comes from Old English duru; bell from Old English belle. Plainly: the bell on the door.

doormat.etymology: door + mat. Door comes from Old English duru; mat from Latin matta (woven straw pad). Together: the mat at the door — its job is to keep the dirt outside.

drain.etymology: From Old English drēahnian, 'to strain out the water, to make dry', tracing back to the Proto-Germanic idea of 'dry'. The core feeling: let the water run away and keep what's dry.

drawer.etymology: The verb draw (to pull) + -er: literally 'a thing that gets pulled out'. The core feeling of a drawer is exactly that concrete: a box that comes out when you pull.

electric-car.etymology: electric + car. Electric comes from Greek ēlektron (amber — rubbing amber makes static electricity); car from Latin carrum. Together: a car driven by electricity, revived by the 21st century's green wave.

electric-cooker.etymology: electric + cooker. Electric comes from Greek ēlektron (amber) — the ancients noticed rubbed amber sparks static, and the word became the root of 'electricity'. Together: a pot that cooks on electric power.

electric-scooter.etymology: electric + scooter. Scooter is scoot (to zip along) + -er. Together: a scooter with a motor — the last-mile ride of modern cities.

employee-id-card.etymology: employee + ID (short for identification) + card. Employee comes from French employé: employ + -ee; identification traces to Latin idem (the same). Together: the card that proves you work here.

envelope.etymology: From French enveloppe, from envelopper (to wrap up): en- (in) + voloper (to wrap, roll). So an envelope is literally 'the thing you wrap something into' — as concrete as it sounds.

eraser.etymology: erase + -er. Erase comes from Latin eradere: e- (out) + radere (to scrape). So an eraser is literally 'the thing that scrapes the writing off' — there's a hint of abrasion in its roots.

extension-cord.etymology: extension + cord. Extension comes from Latin extendere (to stretch out); cord from Greek khordē (string, gut). Together: the cord that stretches your power further.

facial-cleanser.etymology: facial + cleanser. Facial comes from Latin facies (face, appearance); cleanser is cleanse + -er — cleanse carries a stronger 'purify' feeling than clean. Together: the cleanser for your face.

fan.etymology: From Old English fann, tracing back to Latin vannus (a winnowing basket). Farmers tossed grain in a vannus so the wind could carry off the chaff — so a fan has always been 'a tool for making airflow'.

faucet.etymology: From Old French fausset, originally 'the little plug on a barrel', from fausser (to bore through). The core feeling: a small device that plugs, releases, and controls the flow.
faucet.note: fau-cet: turn it and water comes

fennel-seeds.etymology: fennel + seeds. Fennel comes from Old English fenol, tracing back to Latin feniculum ('little hay'), from fenum (hay) — fennel's feathery leaves look like grass. Together: the seeds of the fennel plant.

ferry.etymology: From Old English ferian (to carry, transport), tracing back to Proto-Germanic *farjan (to travel). Fare and fjord share the root. A ferry's core feeling: the service that carries people across the water, again and again.

file-folder.etymology: file + folder. File comes from Latin filum (thread) — documents used to be strung together on a thread for safekeeping; folder is fold + -er. Together: a folded holder for your papers.

filing-cabinet.etymology: filing + cabinet. Filing is file + -ing; cabinet comes from Old French 'little room'. Together: the cabinet where documents get filed away.

fire-hydrant.etymology: fire + hydrant. Hydrant comes from Greek hydōr (water) + -ant. Together: the water valve for fighting fires — the red metal post on the corner.

fire-truck.etymology: fire + truck. Fire comes from Old English fȳr; truck from Greek trokhos (wheel). Together: the truck that fights fires — bright red, carrying hoses and ladders.

fish-sauce.etymology: fish + sauce. Fish comes from Old English fisc; sauce from Latin salsus (salted). Plainly 'a salty fish sauce' — the umami backbone of Vietnamese and Thai cooking.

five-spice-powder.etymology: five + spice + powder. A direct translation of the Chinese 五香粉 — five spices (usually star anise, cassia, cloves, Sichuan pepper, and fennel) balancing the five flavors in one blend.

floor-lamp.etymology: floor + lamp. Floor comes from Old English flōr; lamp from Greek lampas (torch). Together: the lamp that stands on the floor — tall and upright, unlike desk lamps and ceiling lights.

flour.etymology: From Old French flour (flower), meaning 'the finest part' — the whitest, finest part of the grain was called 'the flower of the meal'. Flour and flower share the same root: the choicest layer that milling yields.

flower-bed.etymology: flower + bed. In gardening, bed came to mean 'a planting plot', because a neat patch of flowers looks like a bed made up for them. A flower bed is literally 'a bed for flowers' — one of English's more visual metaphors.

folder.etymology: The verb fold + -er. Fold comes from Old English fealdan (to fold). The core feeling couldn't be more direct: 'a folded thing that wraps around paper'.

food-container.etymology: food + container. Container is contain + -er; contain comes from Latin continere (to hold together). Together: the container that holds your food.

food-processor.etymology: food + processor. Processor is process + -or; process comes from Latin procedere (to go forward). Together: the machine that processes ingredients — chopping, grinding, and mixing in one.

footstool.etymology: foot + stool. Stool comes from Old English stōl, originally 'seat' (cognate with German Stuhl). Together: the little stool for your feet.

fork.etymology: From Old English forca, tracing back to Latin furca (a two-pronged fork). Romans used furca for the farmer's pitchfork; only later did it shrink to the table. The core feeling: a forked point.
fork.note: f-ork: the fork you eat with

freezer.etymology: The verb freeze + -er. Freeze comes from Old English frēosan, tracing back to Proto-Germanic *freusaną. Literally 'the machine that freezes things'.

fridge.etymology: Short for refrigerator: re- (again) + frigerare (to cool, from Latin frigus, cold) + -or. In the 20th century English speakers clipped out the middle of refrigerator and softened the g to dg — and fridge was born.
fridge.note: The casual short form of refrigerator

frozen-food.etymology: frozen (the past participle of freeze) + food. Freeze comes from Old English frēosan. Together: food preserved by freezing — a retail category born when 20th-century freezing technology spread.

frozen-section.etymology: frozen + section. Freeze comes from Old English frēosan; section from Latin sectio (a cutting). Together: the part of the store selling frozen food, usually open freezer chests.

frying-pan.etymology: frying + pan. Pan comes from Old English panne, tracing back to Latin patina (shallow dish). Together: the shallow pan you fry food in.

game-console.etymology: game + console. Console comes from Old French console, originally an architectural term for the carved bracket that supports a shelf, later 'a surface with controls'. Together: the control deck for playing games.

garbage-bag.etymology: garbage + bag. Garbage comes from Old French garbage (poultry offal, kitchen waste); bag from Old Norse baggi. Together: the bag for the trash — same as trash bag.

garbage-truck.etymology: garbage + truck. Garbage comes from Old French garbage (kitchen offal); truck from Greek trokhos (wheel). Together: the truck that collects the trash — a key player in the city's sanitation.

garlic-powder.etymology: garlic + powder. Garlic comes from Old English gārlēac: gār (spear) + lēac (leek) — the cloves look like little spearheads. Together: garlic ground to a powder.

glass.etymology: From Old English glæs, first the material itself, later the cup made from it. Traces back to Proto-Germanic *glasą, possibly related to 'gleaming, amber-colored'.

gloves.etymology: The plural of glove, from Old English glōf, possibly related to the idea of 'palm'. Plural because gloves come in pairs — things that wrap up your hands.

glue.etymology: From Old French glu, tracing back to Late Latin glus (sticky substance) — originally a paste boiled from animal horn and bone. The core feeling: a thick liquid that makes two things stick together.

gondola-lift.etymology: gondola + lift. Gondola comes from the Venetian dialect góndola (little boat) — the cable car's cabin is shaped like a Venetian longboat. Together: an aerial cable car shaped like a Venetian boat.

grater.etymology: The verb grate (to shred by rubbing) + -er. Grate comes from Old French grater (to scrape), tracing back to the Germanic idea of 'scratch'. Together: the tool that scrapes food into fine shreds.

hair-conditioner.etymology: hair + conditioner. Conditioner is condition (to bring into a certain state) + -er. Together: the thing that keeps your hair in good condition.

hair-dryer.etymology: hair + dryer. Dryer is the verb dry + -er, 'a device that makes something dry'. Plainly: the machine that dries your hair.

hairbrush.etymology: hair + brush. Brush comes from Old French broisse, originally brushwood twigs — bundle the twigs and you have a brush. Together: the brush for your hair.

hamper.etymology: From Middle English hanypere, tracing back to Old French hanapier ('a basket for cups'). It later broadened to any big lidded basket — the core feeling is a container you can cover and stash things in.

hand-soap.etymology: hand + soap. Soap comes from Old English sāpe, tracing back to Latin sapo — the Romans learned to make cleansers from fat and ash from the Germanic peoples. Together: soap for your hands.

hand-towel.etymology: hand + towel. Towel comes from Old French toaille, 'a cloth for wiping'. Together: the small cloth for drying your hands.

hanger.etymology: The verb hang + -er: literally 'a thing you hang stuff on'. Hang comes from Old English hangian. The core feeling is direct: it holds your clothes up so they don't wrinkle.

headboard.etymology: head + board. In English head often means 'the front or top end'; board comes from Old English bord (plank). Together: the board at the head of the bed.
headboard.note: head + board = the board at the bed's head

headphones.etymology: head + phones. Phone comes from Greek phōnē (sound). Literally 'sound devices worn on the head' — plural because there's one for each ear.

heater.etymology: The verb heat + -er: literally 'a thing that heats'. Heat comes from Old English hǣtu (warmth), one of the most basic Germanic words.

helicopter.etymology: From Greek helix (spiral) + pteron (wing). So helicopter literally means 'spiral wing' — a 19th-century French coinage that precisely describes the rotating blades on top.

high-speed-train.etymology: high + speed + train. Speed comes from Old English spēd (success, swiftness); train from Old French train (to drag, a series). Together: a train that runs at high speed — like Taiwan's HSR or Japan's Shinkansen.

highlighter.etymology: highlight + -er. Highlight is high + light, originally 'the brightest part' of a painting. So a highlighter is literally 'the pen that makes a passage brightest'.

honey.etymology: From Old English hunig, tracing back to Proto-Germanic *hunangą, possibly related to 'yellow'. So honey carries not just 'sweet' but the golden-yellow image in its roots.
honey.note: hon-ey: the sweet stuff bees make

hook.etymology: From Old English hōc, tracing back to Proto-Germanic *hōkaz — originally just a description of the 'bent' shape. The core feeling is concrete: a curved little thing that catches hold.

hot-air-balloon.etymology: hot + air + balloon. Balloon comes from Italian ballone (big ball), an augmentative of balla (ball). Together: a big ball that rises on hot air — one of humanity's first flying machines.

household-goods-section.etymology: household + goods + section. Household is house + hold; goods is the plural of good ('a good thing'). Together: the area selling everyday household items.

humidifier.etymology: humid + -ify (to make) + -er (agent). Humid comes from Latin humidus (moist), from humere (to be wet). Together: the machine that makes the air moist.

intersection.etymology: From Latin intersectio: inter- (between) + secare (to cut). Literally 'the place where things cut across each other'. So an intersection is where two roads cut across into a cross.

invoice.etymology: From French envoi ('things sent'), from envoyer (to send). So an invoice is at its roots 'the list sent along with the goods' — a bill that accompanies a shipment.

kayak.etymology: From the Inuit qajaq, originally the single-person boat that Arctic peoples built from skins stretched over a wooden frame. English borrowed it directly, so kayak carries the watercraft culture of Arctic hunters.

ketchup.etymology: From the Hokkien kê-tsiap (a brine of pickled fish). 17th-century English traders met this fermented sauce in Southeast Asia; back home the ingredients changed, and 19th-century Americans swapped in tomatoes to make today's ketchup.

kettle.etymology: From Old English cetel, tracing back to Latin catillus (little pot), a diminutive of catinus. The core feeling: a metal vessel for holding and heating water.

keyboard.etymology: key + board. Key comes from Old English cæg (a key), extended to 'a pressed button'; board from Old English bord (plank). Together: a board full of keys.

kitchen-knife.etymology: kitchen + knife. Kitchen comes from Old English cycene, tracing back to Latin coquina (a cooking place); knife from Old English cnīf. Together: the knife used in the kitchen.

knife.etymology: From Old English cnīf (both the c/k are silent — a relic of early English spelling), tracing back to Old Norse knífr. The core feeling: a bladed piece of metal that cuts.
knife.note: The k is silent, ni-fe; plural knives

kombu-powder.etymology: kombu + powder. Kombu is a loanword from Japanese for this large kelp. Together: kombu ground to a powder — rich in natural glutamate, used to add umami.

ladle.etymology: From Old English hlædel: hladan (to load, to scoop up) + -el, literally 'a tool for scooping'. The core feeling is concrete: a long-handled spoon that holds a scoop of liquid.

lamp.etymology: From Greek lampas (torch, lamp), from lampein (to shine, to gleam). So lamp has been tied to the act of shining from the very start — the core feeling couldn't be purer: a thing that glows.

lane.etymology: From Old English lanu, one of the oldest Germanic words, originally just 'a narrow way'. The core feeling is unchanged: the one that's narrower than a road, wider than an alley.
lane.note: l-ane: the traffic lane / narrow way

laptop.etymology: lap + top. Lap comes from Old English læppa (the lap, the fold of a garment). Literally 'a thing that sits on your lap' — highlighting how portable this computer is compared to a desktop.

laundry-basket.etymology: laundry + basket. Laundry comes from Old French lavanderie (a place for washing), tracing back to Latin lavare (to wash). Together: the basket for clothes waiting to be washed.

lid.etymology: From Old English hlid, tracing back to Proto-Germanic *hlidą (a cover). The core feeling is unchanged since ancient times: the piece you set on top.

light-rail.etymology: light + rail. Light comes from Old English lēoht (not heavy); rail from Old French reille (a bar). Together: a rail system lighter than a full train, mostly running at street level in cities.

light-soy-sauce.etymology: light + soy sauce. Soy comes from Japanese shōyu, itself from the Chinese word for soy sauce. Together: soy sauce that's lighter in color and saltier — 生抽 in Cantonese cooking.

living-room-table.etymology: living room + table. Living room literally means 'the room for living', the shared space where family gathers. Together: the table that sits in the living room.

lotion.etymology: From Latin lotio ('a washing'), from lavare (to wash). So lotion first meant 'a liquid for rinsing', and only later became 'a moisturizing lotion for the skin'. The core feeling: a liquid that flows and covers the skin.

magazine.etymology: From Arabic makhāzin (storehouses, the plural of makhzan). 18th-century English publishers pictured a magazine as 'a storehouse loaded with all sorts of articles' — and the metaphor became the word.

mailbox.etymology: mail + box. Mail comes from Old French male (a bag), originally the postman's letter-bag; box from Old English box. Together: the box for receiving and sending letters.

manhole-cover.etymology: manhole + cover. Manhole is man + hole, literally 'a hole a person can climb into' — engineers descend through it to service underground lines. Together: the iron plate that covers the manhole.

marker.etymology: mark + -er. Mark comes from Old English mearc (boundary, sign). So a marker is literally 'a tool for making marks' — a very direct core feeling.

mattress.etymology: From Old French materas, tracing back to Arabic matrah ('a thing thrown down, a mat'). Arabs had a tradition of laying pads on the ground to sleep, and the word entered Europe during the Crusades. The core feeling: the thick pad beneath you as you lie down.

mayonnaise.etymology: From French mayonnaise, possibly from the port of Mahón on the Spanish island of Menorca — 18th-century French troops tasted this egg-yolk sauce there. The word carries a story of a Mediterranean battle and a culinary exchange.

measuring-cup.etymology: measuring + cup. Measure comes from Old French mesurer, tracing back to Latin mensura (a measuring). Together: the cup for measuring portions.

measuring-spoon.etymology: measuring + spoon. Spoon comes from Old English spōn, originally 'a chip or thin slice of wood' — the earliest spoons were curved wooden slivers. Together: the small spoon for measuring portions.

meat-section.etymology: meat + section. Meat comes from Old English mete, which first meant 'food' in general before narrowing to 'animal flesh'. Together: the section that sells meat.

meeting-room.etymology: meeting + room. Meet comes from Old English mētan (to encounter); room from Old English rūm (space). Together: the space where a group meets.

membership-card.etymology: membership + card. Member comes from Latin membrum (a limb, a member); card from Greek khartēs (papyrus). Together: the card that proves you're a member.

micellar-water.etymology: micellar + water. Micelle comes from Latin micella, a diminutive of mica (a crumb, a speck). So micellar water is literally 'water holding tiny oil specks' — it looks like water but grabs dirt the way oil does.

microphone.etymology: micro- (tiny) + -phone (sound). Both roots are Greek: mikros (small), phōnē (sound). Literally 'a device that captures tiny sounds' — a microphone amplifies even the faintest sound.

microwave.etymology: micro- (tiny) + wave. Micro comes from Greek mikros (small); wave from Old English wafian (to wave). Literally 'a tiny wave' — a wavelength shorter than ordinary electromagnetic waves, which makes food molecules vibrate and heat up.

minibus.etymology: mini- (small) + bus. Mini is short for miniature, from Latin minium (red lead, extended to 'a tiny painting'); bus is short for omnibus. Together: a small bus.

mirin.etymology: From Japanese 味醂 (mirin): mi- (flavor) + -rin (sweetness). It's the key seasoning that lends sweetness and gloss to Japanese cooking, and its name reflects that core of 'a sweet-tasting seasoning'.

mirror.etymology: From Old French mireor, tracing back to Latin mirare (to gaze, to wonder) — the same root as miracle. The core feeling: the smooth surface that makes you gaze at yourself in wonder.

miso.etymology: From Japanese 味噌 (miso), a Heian-period word possibly from a related Korean term or an early Chinese form of 'paste'. The core feeling: a fermented bean paste with a deep, savory saltiness.

mobile-phone.etymology: mobile + phone. Mobile comes from Latin mobilis, from movere (to move); phone is short for telephone. Together: a phone that can move — as opposed to the fixed-line landline.

moisturizer.etymology: moisture + -ize (to make) + -er (agent): literally 'the thing that keeps something moist'. Moisture comes from Old French moistour, tracing back to Latin mustum (freshly pressed grape juice) — the core feeling is always 'wet'.

mold-remover.etymology: mold + remover. Remove comes from Old French remouvoir (to move away): re- (again, thoroughly) + move. Together: the thing that thoroughly moves mold away.

monitor.etymology: From Latin monitor, from monere (to remind, to warn). So monitor originally meant 'one who reminds', later extended to 'a screen that shows you what's going on' — the display keeps reporting to you.
monitor.note: Monitor also means 'to watch over'; the display screen

monorail.etymology: mono- (single) + rail. Mono comes from Greek monos (alone); rail from Old French reille (a bar). Together: a railway with just one rail — common at theme parks and airports.

motorcycle.etymology: motor + cycle. Motor comes from Latin movere (to move); cycle from Greek kyklos (wheel). Together: a two-wheeler with a motor — the new vehicle that appeared when engines were bolted onto bicycles in the late 19th century.

mouse.etymology: Borrowed from the animal mouse, from Old English mūs. When the device was invented in the 1960s, engineers thought its shape plus the cord trailing behind looked like a little mouse — so they just borrowed the word.
mouse.note: Looks like a mouse trailing a tail (the cord)

mouse-pad.etymology: mouse + pad. Pad comes from Low German pad (a small flat soft piece). Together: the little pad for your mouse, so it glides smoothly and doesn't slip.

mouthwash.etymology: mouth + wash. Both are basic Old English words — mouth from mūth, wash from wæscan. Together: the water you rinse your mouth with. As plain as it gets.

mrt.etymology: Short for Mass Rapid Transit. Mass (large-scale) comes from Latin massa (a lump); rapid from Latin rapidus (fast); transit from Latin transitus (a crossing). Together: a mass rapid transit system.

msg.etymology: Short for monosodium glutamate: mono- (single) + sodium + glutamate. In 1908 the Japanese chemist Kikunae Ikeda isolated it from kombu, giving the fifth taste — umami — a chemical identity.
msg.note: MSG is short for monosodium glutamate; say the three letters separately.

mug.etymology: From Old Norse mugge or Low German mokke, originally 'a round-bellied vessel'. The core feeling: a sturdy, thick drinking vessel with a handle — heftier than an ordinary cup.
mug.note: m-ug: the big cup with a handle

mustard.etymology: From Old French mostarde, tracing back to Latin mustum (unfermented grape juice) — ancient Romans ground mustard seeds into fresh wine, so a bit of winemaking history hides in the name.

nail-clipper.etymology: nail + clipper. Clipper is clip + -er; clip originally meant 'to cut off, to grip'. Together: the little tool for clipping nails.

newspaper.etymology: news + paper. News is the plural of new ('new things from every quarter'); paper comes from Latin papyrus. Plainly: paper printed with the news.

newsstand.etymology: news + stand. News is the plural of new ('new things'); stand comes from the verb stand, 'a little table you use standing up'. Together: the little stall that sells newspapers.

nightstand.etymology: night + stand. Stand comes from the verb stand, 'a little table you use standing up'. Together: the little table you keep by the bed at night.

non-slip-mat.etymology: non- (not) + slip + mat. Slip comes from Middle English slippen (to slide). Literally 'a mat that won't slip' — as direct as it gets.
non-slip-mat.note: non (not) + slip + mat = the anti-slip mat

notebook.etymology: note + book. Note comes from Latin nota (a mark); book from Old English bōc (possibly related to 'beech' — the ancients wrote on beech-wood slats). Together: the book for jotting down key points.

notepad.etymology: note + pad. Pad extended from 'a flat block' to 'a stack of paper'. Together: the little pad for short notes — usually smaller and more casual than a notebook.

office-chair.etymology: office + chair. Office comes from Latin officium (duty, service); chair from Old French chaiere (seat). Together: the chair you sit in for office work.

office-supplies.etymology: office + supplies. Supply comes from Latin supplere (to fill up): sub- (below) + plere (to fill). Together: the goods that fill an office's needs.

olive-oil.etymology: olive + oil. Olive comes from Latin oliva and Greek elaiā; oil from Latin oleum, itself a derivative of elaiā. So the compound is really 'olive + the thing that comes from olives' — a nod to the olive's central place in Mediterranean culture.

onion-powder.etymology: onion + powder. Onion comes from Old French oignon and Latin unio (oneness) — because an onion packs layer upon layer into one. Together: onion ground to a powder.

oregano.etymology: From Greek origanon: oros (mountain) + ganos (joy), literally 'joy of the mountains' — the herb grows on mountain slopes and its scent delights. So there's a bit of poetry in oregano's roots.

oven.etymology: From Old English ofen, tracing back to Proto-Germanic *uhnaz, possibly cognate with Latin aulla (pot). The core feeling has always been 'an enclosed chamber that gives off heat'.

oyster-sauce.etymology: oyster + sauce. Oyster comes from Old French oistre and Latin ostrea. Legend has it that the 19th-century Cantonese cook Lee Kum Sheung forgot to turn off the heat while boiling oysters and accidentally simmered them into a thick, savory sauce — and oyster sauce was born.

pajamas.etymology: From Persian/Urdu pāy-jāmah, literally 'leg (pāy) garment (jāmah)' — originally the loose trousers of South Asia. British colonists carried the word back to Europe, where it became the word for sleepwear. The core feeling remains 'loose, soft trousers'.

pan.etymology: From Old English panne, tracing back to Latin patina (a shallow dish). The core feeling: a shallow-bottomed vessel you can set over a flame.

paper.etymology: From Latin papyrus, the writing material the ancient Egyptians pressed from papyrus reeds. So paper's roots point straight to humanity's earliest writing medium — a water plant from the banks of the Nile.

paper-clip.etymology: paper + clip. Clip comes from Old English clyppan (to embrace, grip). Together: the little thing that grips paper — the familiar looped shape is a late-19th-century design.

paper-shredder.etymology: paper + shredder. Shred comes from Old English scrēade (a fragment, a snipped strip); turned into a verb plus -er, it literally means 'the machine that cuts things into strips'.

paper-towel.etymology: paper + towel. Paper comes from Latin papyrus; towel from Old French toaille (a cloth for wiping). Together: a disposable towel made of paper.

park.etymology: From Old French parc, tracing back to Medieval Latin parricus (an enclosure, a reserve). Originally an enclosed hunting ground reserved for nobles, it later opened to the public as a park. So park carries the history of 'a set-aside patch of nature'.
park.note: p-ark: the park (as a verb, 'to park')

parking-lot.etymology: parking + lot. Park developed its 'to park a vehicle' sense in the 19th century; lot comes from Old English hlot (a share), extended to 'a designated plot of land'. Together: the plot designated for parking.

parking-meter.etymology: parking + meter. Meter comes from Greek metron (measure). Together: the machine that times your parking — first installed in Oklahoma, USA in 1935.

parking-space.etymology: parking + space. Space comes from Latin spatium (space, distance). Together: one car's parking slot, a unit marked out with painted lines.

parsley.etymology: From Old English petersilie, tracing back to Greek petroselinon: petros (rock) + selinon (celery) — because the herb grows among rocks. So parsley hides the image of 'celery in the rock crevices' in its roots.

peanut-butter.etymology: peanut + butter. Peanut is pea + nut; butter comes from Greek boutyron, originally 'cow dairy'. Together: a peanut paste as smooth as butter.

pedestrian.etymology: From Latin pedester (going on foot), from the root pes/ped- (foot). So pedestrian literally means 'a person using their feet' — one who walks rather than drives or rides. Same root as pedal, pedicure, pedestal.

pedestrian-bridge.etymology: pedestrian + bridge. Pedestrian comes from Latin pes (foot); bridge from Old English brycg. Together: a bridge for people, as opposed to a road bridge.

pedestrian-button.etymology: pedestrian + button. Button comes from Old French boton, originally 'a clothing button', later 'a little device you press'. Together: the button pedestrians press.

peeler.etymology: The verb peel + -er. Peel comes from Old French peler, tracing back to Latin pilare (to remove hair, to strip), from pilus (hair). Together: the tool for peeling.

pen.etymology: From Old French penne, tracing back to Latin penna (feather). The ancients wrote by dipping a goose quill in ink, so pen literally means 'quill'. Even though modern pens have nothing to do with feathers, the word preserves that history of writing.

pepper.etymology: From Old English pipor, via Latin piper and Greek peperi, ultimately from Sanskrit pippali. The word traveled the ancient spice roads from India across Eurasia — one of humanity's oldest seasonings.

perfume.etymology: From Latin per fumum, 'through smoke' — the ancients burned incense in offerings, and the scent drifted off with the smoke. So perfume first meant 'the fragrance in the smoke', later the liquid scent. The core feeling is still drifting fragrance.

pharmacy.etymology: From Greek pharmakon, meaning 'drug, poison, or spell' — the ancient Greeks saw healing and poisoning as two sides of the same knowledge. So pharmacy carries the mysterious aura of the old herbalist in its roots.

photo-frame.etymology: photo + frame. Photo is short for photograph, from Greek phōs (light) + graphē (drawing); frame from Old English framian (to provide support). Together: the support frame for a photo.

photocopier.etymology: photo- (of light) + copier. Photo comes from Greek phōs (light); copier is copy + -er. Together: the machine that copies documents with light — a photocopier works by shining light and reproducing the image.

picture-frame.etymology: picture + frame. Picture comes from Latin pictura (a painting, from pingere, to paint), the same root as paint; frame from Old English framian (to support). Together: the support that frames a picture.

pillow.etymology: From Old English pyle, tracing back to Latin pulvinus (a cushion). Romans already rested their heads on cushions while lying down, so the core feeling of pillow is unchanged: a soft block that supports your head.
pillow.note: pil-low: cushions your head in sleep

pillowcase.etymology: pillow + case. Case comes from Old French casse, tracing back to Latin capsa (box, container). Together: the layer of cloth that cases the pillow.

plastic-bag.etymology: plastic + bag. Plastic comes from Greek plastikos (able to be molded), from plassein (to mold); bag from Old Norse baggi. Together: a bag made of plastic — the container that spread after the 20th century.

plastic-wrap.etymology: plastic + wrap. Plastic comes from Greek plastikos (moldable); wrap from Middle English wrappen (to wrap). Together: the plastic film you wrap food in.

plate.etymology: From Old French plat (flat, a flat dish), tracing back to Greek platys (broad and flat). The core feeling is 'a flat, thin piece' — the exact opposite of the bowl's 'half a sphere'.
plate.note: pl-ate: the flat dish for food

police-car.etymology: police + car. Police comes from Greek polis (city-state), originally 'the governance of the city'; car from Latin carrum. Together: the car police use on duty, usually with lights and a radio.

post-office.etymology: post + office. Post comes from Latin positus (placed) — relay stations were 'placed' along the roads; office from Latin officium (duty). Together: the place where postal work is done.

pot.etymology: From Old English pott, possibly cognate with Low German pot, meaning 'a deep vessel'. The core feeling: a deep-bottomed container that holds more liquid — the counterpart to the shallow, flat pan.

potato-starch.etymology: potato + starch. Potato comes from Spanish patata (a blend of batata, sweet potato, and papa, potato); starch from Old English stercan (to stiffen). Together: starch extracted from potatoes.

potted-plant.etymology: potted (the adjective from pot) + plant. Pot comes from Old English pott (vessel); plant from Latin planta (a sprout, a shoot). Together: a plant grown in a pot.

power-lines.etymology: power + lines. Power comes from Old French poeir (ability); line from Latin linea (thread). Together: the lines that carry electricity, strung on poles to connect everywhere.

power-outlet.etymology: power + outlet. Outlet is out + let, literally 'an opening that lets something out'. Together: the opening where electricity comes out of the wall.

price-tag.etymology: price + tag. Price comes from Old French pris (value); tag from Middle English tagge (a small hanging strip). Together: the little tag on an item that shows its price.

printer.etymology: print + -er. Print comes from Old French priente (an impressed mark), from Latin premere (to press). So a printer is literally 'the machine that presses things out'.

produce-section.etymology: produce + section. Produce comes from Latin producere (to bring forth): pro- (forward) + ducere (to lead), extended to 'what the land brings forth'. Together: the section selling the land's fresh goods.

projector.etymology: project + -or. Project comes from Latin proicere: pro- (forward) + jacere (to throw). So a projector literally 'throws the image forward' — a vivid core feeling.

projector-screen.etymology: projector + screen. Screen comes from Old French escren, originally 'a screen against the wind'. Together: the screen a projector casts its image onto.

quilt.etymology: From French duvet, originally meaning down feathers. The word came to mean a soft bed covering filled with down or similar material.
quilt.note: duvet: the soft filled bed cover

range-hood.etymology: range + hood. Range comes from Old French renge (a row), originally 'a row of stoves'; hood from Old English hōd (a cowl, a cover). Together: the hood that hangs over the stove.

razor.etymology: From Old French rasor, tracing back to Latin radere (to scrape, to shave). The same root gives us erase — the core feeling is 'scraping something off close against the surface'.

receipt.etymology: From Latin receptum (received), from recipere (to take back, to receive): re- (again) + capere (to take). So a receipt is literally 'proof of what was received' — the seller's confirmation that the money came in.
receipt.note: The p in receipt is silent.

reception-desk.etymology: reception + desk. Reception comes from Latin receptio (a receiving), from recipere (to receive, to welcome). Together: the desk where visitors are welcomed.

recliner.etymology: recline + -er. Recline comes from Latin reclinare: re- (back) + clinare (to lean). Together: a chair that lets you lean back.

refrigerated-section.etymology: refrigerated + section. Refrigerate comes from Latin refrigerare: re- (again) + frigerare (to cool). Together: the section of goods kept cold but not frozen.

remote.etymology: Short for remote control, 'control from a distance'. Remote comes from Latin remotus (moved away): re- (back) + movere (to move). The core feeling: operating something from a distance, not up close.

remote-control-holder.etymology: remote control + holder. Holder is the verb hold + -er. Together: the container that holds your remote controls.

restaurant.etymology: From French restaurant, from restaurer (to restore, to refresh). In 18th-century Paris a shop selling restorative broths claimed to 'restore' your strength (restaurant), and restaurant came to mean 'a place where a meal restores you'.

reusable-bag.etymology: re- (again) + usable + bag. Usable is use + -able; use comes from Latin usus. Together: a bag you can use again and again — the eco-conscious replacement for single-use plastic.

rice-cooker.etymology: rice + cooker. Rice comes from Old French ris, via Greek oryza (ultimately from an Indian language); cooker is cook + -er. Together: the pot that cooks rice.

rice-vinegar.etymology: rice + vinegar. Rice comes via Greek oryza from an Indian language; vinegar is French vin aigre (sour wine). Together: rice fermented into a sour seasoning — the source of the light tang in East Asian cooking.

rice-wine.etymology: rice + wine. Rice entered Europe via Greek oryza; wine comes from Latin vinum. Together: wine brewed from fermented rice — the counterpart to grape wine.

rickshaw.etymology: From the Japanese 人力車 (jin-riki-sha), clipped into English as rickshaw. It literally means 'a human-powered vehicle', spreading from Japan across Asia in the late 19th century.

road.etymology: From Old English rād, originally 'a riding, a journey', the same root as the verb ride. So road hides the image of 'a long way you can ride a horse down' — the core feeling is a long strip connecting far-off places.

roadblock.etymology: road + block. Block comes from Old French bloc (a lump, a wooden block). Together: something set across the road — a stone, a barrier, or a police checkpoint.

robe.etymology: Dressing refers to getting dressed; gown comes from Old French goune, a long garment. Together, dressing gown means a loose garment worn over sleepwear at home.
robe.note: dressing + gown: a gown worn over sleepwear

robot-vacuum.etymology: robot + vacuum. Robot comes from Czech robota (forced labor), coined by the writer Karel Čapek in 1920; vacuum from Latin vacuus (empty). Together: a robot that vacuums the floor by itself.

rock-sugar.etymology: rock + sugar. Rock comes from Old French roque (rock); sugar from Arabic sukkar and Sanskrit śarkarā. The image is 'sugar shaped like rock' — rock sugar's crystals are big and mineral-like.

rocket.etymology: From Italian rocchetta (a little spindle), a diminutive of rocca (spindle) — early gunpowder rockets were shaped like the bobbins used for spinning thread. So rocket hides the fun image of 'a little fire-spitting spindle' in its roots.

roller-skates.etymology: roller + skates. Roller is roll + -er; skate comes from Dutch schaats (a stilt, a skate). Together: skates fitted with rollers — unlike ice skates, they glide on land.

rosemary.etymology: From Latin ros marinus: ros (dew) + marinus (of the sea), literally 'dew of the sea' — rosemary grows on the hills along the Mediterranean coast. So its roots hold an image of sea breeze and morning dew.
rosemary.note: rose + mary, but unrelated to roses

roundabout.etymology: round + about. Round comes from Old French roond (round); about from Old English onbūtan (around). Literally 'going around in a circle' — exactly how you drive a roundabout.

router.etymology: route + -er. Route comes from Old French rute, tracing back to Latin rupta (a broken-open way). Together: the machine that routes data — the core feeling is 'directing and forwarding'.

rug.etymology: From the Scandinavian branch (Old Norse rǫgg, 'shaggy tuft'), originally 'a coarse woolen fabric'. So a rug's core feeling is 'a thick, tufted small textile you tread on' — as opposed to the wall-to-wall carpet.

ruler.etymology: rule + -er. Rule comes from Latin regula (a straight stick, a standard). So ruler means both 'one who sets the rules' and 'the tool for drawing lines' — 'setting boundaries' is the core feeling.
ruler.note: rule (line/rule) + er = the measuring ruler (also 'a ruler' who governs)

sailboat.etymology: sail + boat. Sail comes from Old English segl, the same root as sea; boat from Old English bāt. Together: a boat that runs on a sail — one of humanity's oldest forms of long-distance transport.

sake.etymology: From Japanese 酒 (sake), originally the general word for alcoholic drinks, which in English came to mean specifically Japanese rice wine. The word keeps the whole feel of Japanese drinking culture — a stronger cultural identity than the plain 'rice wine'.

sale.etymology: From Old English sala, tracing back to Proto-Germanic *salō (a giving, a handing over). So sale's core is the act of 'handing something over (for money)' — the modern sense of 'discount selling' came later.

salt.etymology: From Old English sealt, tracing all the way to Proto-Indo-European *sal- — one of humanity's oldest words. Roman soldiers were paid in salt (salarium), which is why salary shares this root — a sign of how precious salt once was.

sanitary-pad.etymology: sanitary + pad. Sanitary comes from Latin sanitas (health), the same root as sane. Together: an absorbent pad designed for health and hygiene.

scale.etymology: From Old Norse skál, originally 'a bowl, a dish' — the two ends of an ancient balance were dishes you set things on to see which side sank. So scale's core feeling is 'weighing two pans against each other'; modern digital scales have no pans, but the sense of 'measuring' remains.
scale.note: Scale also means the weighing scale

scanner.etymology: scan + -er. Scan comes from Latin scandere (to climb, to read verse line by line). So a scanner's core feeling is 'sweeping across line by line, capturing the image'.

school-bus.etymology: school + bus. School comes from Greek skholē (leisure, discussion) — the ancient Greeks saw learning as a leisure activity; bus is short for omnibus. Together: the bus that carries students to and from school — America's bright yellow school bus being the classic image.

scissors.etymology: From Old French cisoires, tracing back to Late Latin cisoria, from caedere (to cut). Plural because scissors are made of 'two blades' — neither works without the other.
scissors.note: Usually plural; one is 'a pair of scissors'

scooter.etymology: The verb scoot (to move fast, to dart off) + -er. Scoot possibly comes from Old Norse skjota (to shoot, to propel). So scooter literally means 'a thing that glides fast'.

seafood-section.etymology: seafood + section. Sea comes from Old English sǣ; food from Old English fōda. 'Food from the sea' plus 'section' gives 'the corner that sells seafood'.

seasoning-jar.etymology: seasoning + jar. Season comes from Old French saison, originally 'a season of the year', extended to 'adding flavor suited to the season'; jar from Arabic jarrah (an earthen pot). Together: the jar that holds seasonings.

security-camera.etymology: security + camera. Security comes from Latin securitas (freedom from care); camera from Latin camera (a vaulted room, later extended to the camera). Together: a camera set up for security.

self-checkout-machine.etymology: self + checkout + machine. Self comes from Old English self; checkout is check (to verify) + out. Together: the machine you check out at yourself — retail's 21st-century labor substitute.

sesame-oil.etymology: sesame + oil. Sesame comes from Greek sēsamon, ultimately probably Semitic. Together: oil pressed from sesame seeds — the key finishing oil that adds aroma to East Asian cooking.

sesame-paste.etymology: sesame + paste. Paste comes from Late Latin pasta (a doughy mass, the same root as pasta). Together: sesame ground into a paste — the heart of cold noodles and sesame noodles.

set-top-box.etymology: set (short for TV set) + top + box. Originally this box literally sat on top of the TV set, so the name is very direct: 'the box that sits on top of the set'.

shacha-sauce.etymology: Shacha comes from the Hokkien 沙茶 (sa-te), possibly a cousin of the Southeast Asian satay. Chinese emigrants brought it back to the Chaoshan region, where it was localized into today's savory-salty-spicy sauce made from dried shrimp and spices.

shampoo.etymology: From Hindi/Urdu chāmpo, meaning 'to massage, to knead'. 18th-century Britons in India saw the local scalp massage and carried the word home, where it later came to mean 'hair-washing liquid'. The core feeling still carries the act of 'kneading the head'.

shaving-cream.etymology: shaving + cream. Shave comes from Old English sceafan (to scrape, to shave); cream from Old French cresme, tracing back to Latin chrisma (an ointment). Together: the creamy stuff you apply while shaving.

shelf.etymology: From Middle Low German schelf, originally 'a flat ledge of rock'. So shelf's core feeling has always been 'a horizontal board' — a ledge you can set things on.

shichimi.etymology: From Japanese 七味 (shichimi): shichi (seven) + mi (flavor). It's a spice blend invented by Edo-period herbal-medicine sellers, balancing seven spices (chili, sansho pepper, dried tangerine peel, hemp, poppy seed, nori, ginger).

shop.etymology: From Old English sceoppa, originally 'a small booth or stall'. So shop has always felt friendlier and more casual than store — its core feeling is 'a small owner-run storefront', as opposed to the warehouse-like store.

shopping-basket.etymology: shopping + basket. Shop comes from Old English sceoppa (a small shop), plus -ing; basket from Old French baschoe. Together: the basket you carry your goods in while browsing.

shopping-cart.etymology: shopping + cart. Cart comes from Old Norse kartr (a small wagon). Together: the cart for shopping — invented by an American supermarket in 1937 to get customers to buy more.

shower.etymology: From Old English scūr, originally 'a brief rain shower'. It was later borrowed to describe 'a stream of water falling from above', so the shower you bathe in is, at its core, 'a man-made little rain'.
shower.note: show + er; rinsing like rain from the sky

shower-curtain.etymology: shower + curtain. Curtain comes from Old French cortine, tracing back to Latin cortina (an enclosing screen). Together: the waterproof curtain that encloses the shower.

shower-curtain-rod.etymology: shower + curtain + rod. Rod comes from Old English rodd, originally 'a slender straight stick'. Together: the rod the shower curtain hangs from.

shower-head.etymology: shower + head. In English head often means 'the topmost or foremost part' — head of a pin, head of an arrow. Together: the foremost water-releasing part of the shower fixture.

shower-room.etymology: shower + room. Room comes from Old English rūm (space, room). Together: the small space for showering.

sichuan-peppercorn.etymology: Sichuan + peppercorn. Sichuan is the pinyin for the Chinese province; peppercorn is pepper + corn (a grain). Literally 'a Sichuan peppercorn' — but it's unrelated to true pepper, and its tingling comes from its own hydroxy-sanshool.

side-table.etymology: side + table. Side comes from Old English sīde (a side); table from Latin tabula (board). Together: the little table set off to the side.

sidewalk.etymology: side + walk. Side comes from Old English sīde; walk from Old English wealcan (to walk). Plainly: the place to walk beside the road. British English calls it the pavement.

signboard.etymology: sign + board. Sign comes from Latin signum (a mark, a signal); board from Old English bord (plank). Together: a board hung out to display a sign — a shop's face to its customers.

sink.etymology: From the verb sink (to go down), Old English sincan. A sink first meant 'the hole where wastewater sinks into the ground', later shifting to 'the basin above'. So the word still carries the image of 'water flowing down'.
sink.note: sink: the basin water runs down; as a verb, 'to sink'

skateboard.etymology: skate + board. Skate comes from Dutch schaats (an ice skate); board from Old English bord (plank). Together: a board you can glide on — the new sport 1950s California surfers invented by bolting wheels onto a surfboard.

slippers.etymology: The plural of slipper, from the verb slip (to slide in easily) + -er, literally 'a thing you slip your foot into'. The core feeling: the comfort of 'no laces, just slide your foot in'.

slotted-spoon.etymology: slotted + spoon. Slot comes from Old French esclot (a slit, a groove); spoon from Old English spōn (a wood chip). Together: a spoon with slits — its whole point is 'lifting out the solids and letting the liquid drain through'.
slotted-spoon.note: slotted + spoon = the spoon with holes

smoke-detector.etymology: smoke + detector. Detect comes from Latin detegere (to uncover): de- (off) + tegere (to cover). Literally 'the thing that uncovers smoke'.

snack-section.etymology: snack + section. Snack comes from Middle Dutch snacken (to bite, to snap) — originally a verb, later 'a light bite to eat'. Together: the section that sells snacks.

soap.etymology: From Old English sāpe, tracing back to Latin sapo — the Romans learned to make a cleanser from animal fat and wood ash from the Germanic peoples. The core feeling: a solid block that lathers up and carries dirt away.
soap.note: so-ap: for washing hands and body

sofa.etymology: From Arabic ṣuffa, originally 'a long stone bench laid with cushions'. It entered Europe with Arab culture and became the modern padded couch. The core feeling remains 'a long soft seat for several people side by side'.

soy-sauce.etymology: soy + sauce. Soy comes from Japanese shōyu, itself from the Chinese word for soy sauce; sauce from Latin salsus (salted). The compound traces the seasoning's route from China through Japan to Europe.

spatula.etymology: From Latin spatula, a diminutive of spatha (a broad flat sword or blade). So a spatula's core feeling is 'a little flat broad blade' — one that can reach the bottom of the pan and lift food out.

speaker.etymology: The verb speak + -er, literally 'a thing that speaks'. Speak comes from Old English sprecan. The core feeling is charming: it turns invisible electrical signals into sound — as if the machine were speaking.
speaker.note: speak (make sound) + er = the loudspeaker (also 'a speaker' who talks)

speedboat.etymology: speed + boat. Speed comes from Old English spēd (success, swiftness); boat from Old English bāt. Together: a boat that goes fast — emphasizing engine power and pace over the ordinary pleasure yacht.

sponge.etymology: From Greek spongos, originally the porous sea creature itself. The ancients found dried sponges soaked up water wonderfully and used them for cleaning; synthetic sponges came later. The core feeling: a porous thing that drinks up lots of liquid.
