spoon.etymology: From Old English spōn, originally 'a wood chip, a thin sliver' — the earliest spoons were a scooped-out piece of wood. So spoon's core feeling hides the prototype of 'a curved little wood chip'.

sports-car.etymology: sports + car. Sport comes from Old French desport (pastime, fun), from disportare (to carry away, away from cares); car from Latin carrum. Together: a car built for the joy of driving — all about handling and speed.

squeegee.etymology: From the verb squeege (19th-century English slang for 'to press'), probably a variant of squeeze. The core feeling: a tool you press against a surface to push the water away.

stapler.etymology: staple + -er. Staple comes from Old English stapol (a post, a support), originally a U-shaped prop. Together: the tool that presses U-shaped staples into paper.

staples.etymology: The plural of staple, from Old English stapol (a post, a support), originally a U-shaped wooden post. It later shrank to today's metal staple, but the basic U shape has survived.
staples.note: The staples a stapler uses; usually plural

star-anise.etymology: star + anise. Anise comes from Greek anison, a Mediterranean spice; star anise is shaped like an eight-pointed star, so Europeans named it 'star-shaped anise' — though botanically the two are unrelated, they merely taste alike.

station.etymology: From Latin statio (a standing, a standing-place), from stare (to stand). So station literally means 'the place where vehicles stand' — a fixed point where they stop to let people on and off.

steamer-basket.etymology: steamer + basket. Steam comes from Old English stēam (vapor); basket from Old French baschoe. Together: the basket you set food in to steam — its core feeling is 'letting the steam pass through the food'.

sticky-notes.etymology: sticky + notes. Sticky comes from stick (to adhere); note from Latin nota (a mark). Together: little notes that stick — invented by 3M in the 1970s and now an office standard.

stop-sign.etymology: stop + sign. Stop comes from Old English stoppian; sign from Latin signum. Together: the sign that tells you to stop — the octagonal red design is an international standard.

storage-box.etymology: storage + box. Storage is store + -age; store comes from Old French estore (equipment, provisions). Together: the box for storing things.

stove.etymology: From Middle Low German stove, originally 'a heated room' (a warming room). It later narrowed to the heater/cooker within the room, and finally became today's stovetop.

strainer.etymology: The verb strain + -er. Strain comes from Old French estreindre (to grip tightly, to press), tracing back to Latin stringere (to draw tight). So a strainer is literally 'the tool that presses liquid through to filter it'.

street.etymology: From Old English strǣt, tracing back to Late Latin strata via (a paved road) — the Romans paved roads with stone, and the surface was 'laid out flat' (strata is the past participle of sternere, to lay). So street carries the mark of Roman road engineering.

street-sign.etymology: street + sign. Street comes from the Roman 'paved road'; sign from Latin signum. Together: the sign that marks a street's name — a wayfinding aid in the city.

street-vendor.etymology: street + vendor. Vendor comes from Latin vendere (to sell). Together: a seller with a stall on the street — the street-hawker culture common in cities.

streetlight.etymology: street + light. Street comes from the Roman 'paved road'; light from Old English lēoht. Together: the light on the street — the city infrastructure that lights the road at night.

submarine.etymology: sub- (beneath) + marine (of the sea). Sub- comes from Latin 'under'; marine from Latin mare (sea). Literally 'the underwater thing' — first an adjective, later the noun for 'a ship that sails beneath the sea'.

subway.etymology: sub- (beneath) + way. Sub comes from Latin 'under'; way from Old English weg (road). Literally 'the underground way' — the North American word for the metro, called the underground in British English.

subway-station.etymology: subway + station. Subway is sub- (beneath) + way, literally 'the underground way'; station comes from Latin 'a standing-place'. Together: the station where the subway stops.

sugar.etymology: From Old French sukre, via Arabic sukkar and Persian shakar, ultimately from Sanskrit śarkarā (grit, sugar grains). The word's path perfectly retraces sugar's journey from India through the Middle East to Europe.

supermarket.etymology: super- (super) + market. Super comes from Latin 'above, beyond'; market from Latin mercatus (trade). Together: a store on a scale beyond the ordinary market — the retail model developed in 20th-century America.

sweet-chili-sauce.etymology: sweet + chili + sauce. Sweet comes from Old English swēte; chili from Nahuatl chīlli; sauce from Latin salsus (salted). Together: a sauce that's sweet with a chili kick — a Thai-cooking staple.

table-knife.etymology: table + knife. Table comes from Latin tabula (board); knife from Old English cnīf. Together: the knife used at the dining table — usually blunter than a sharp kitchen knife.

table-lamp.etymology: table + lamp. Table comes from Latin tabula (board); lamp from Greek lampas (torch). Together: the small lamp that sits on a table.

tampon.etymology: From French tampon, originally 'a plug, a soft thing that stops a bottle'. The French comes from a Germanic idea of 'plug'. The core feeling: a small thing you insert that absorbs liquid.

tape.etymology: From Old English tæppe, 'a narrow strip of cloth'. Originally a thin band of fabric, it later shifted to the sticky plastic or paper strip. The core feeling is unchanged: 'a long strip'.

taxi.etymology: Short for taximeter cab. Taximeter is taxe (a fare rate) + meter (a measure), the device that precisely calculates the fare; cab is short for cabriolet (a one-horse carriage). So taxi literally means 'a fare-metering carriage'.

taxi-stand.etymology: taxi + stand. Taxi is short for taximeter cab (a fare-metering carriage); stand comes from the verb stand, 'a waiting place'. Together: the place where taxis wait for fares.

teapot.etymology: tea + pot. Tea comes from the Hokkien tê, which Dutch traders carried from Fujian to Europe; pot from Old English pott. Together: the pot for brewing tea.

telephone.etymology: tele- (far) + -phone (sound). Both roots are Greek: tele is 'distant', phōnē is 'sound'. Literally 'the far-off voice' — the 19th-century inventors' most poetic name for the phone.

thick-soy-sauce.etymology: thick + soy sauce. Thick comes from Old English þicce (dense). Together: soy sauce thickened with sugar or starch, richer than the ordinary kind — 醬油膏 in Taiwan.

thyme.etymology: From Greek thymon, possibly related to the verb thyein (to burn, to sacrifice) — the ancient Greeks burned this herb as temple incense. So thyme carries the ancient ritual feeling of 'incense offered to the gods'.
thyme.note: The th in thyme is silent — it sounds like time.

tissue.etymology: From Old French tissu, meaning 'woven fabric', from the verb tistre (to weave), from Latin texere (to weave, the same root as textile). It first meant a light fabric, later shifting to 'paper as thin as woven cloth'.

toaster.etymology: The verb toast + -er. Toast comes from Old French toster, tracing back to Latin torrere (to parch, to dry). Literally 'the machine that toasts things'.

toilet.etymology: From French toilette, originally 'a little cloth' (toile is cloth, -ette is the diminutive) — the small cloth laid on the table for grooming. It came to mean 'the grooming process', and finally, euphemistically, 'the toilet'.

toilet-brush.etymology: toilet + brush. Brush comes from Old French broisse, originally brushwood twigs bundled together. Together: the long-handled brush for scrubbing the toilet.

toilet-paper.etymology: toilet + paper. Paper comes from Latin papyrus (the papyrus reed the ancient Egyptians wrote on, which gave paper its name). Plainly: paper for the toilet.

toilet-seat.etymology: toilet + seat. Seat comes from Old Norse sæti, originally 'a place to sit'. Together: the ring you sit on atop the toilet.

toilet-tank.etymology: toilet + tank. Tank comes from Portuguese tanque (a reservoir), possibly tracing further to an Indian regional language. The core feeling is 'a water-holding container' — here, the water tank behind the toilet.

tongs.etymology: From Old English tang/tange, 'a thing that bites', tracing back to Proto-Germanic *tangō. Plural because tongs are made of two arms, neither working alone. The core feeling: 'a thing that bites and grips'.

toothbrush.etymology: tooth + brush. Tooth comes from Old English tōth, one of the oldest Indo-European words; brush from the Old French idea of a bundle of twigs. Together: the little brush for your teeth.

toothpaste.etymology: tooth + paste. Paste comes from Late Latin pasta, originally a doughy soft mass (the same word as pasta). Together: the paste you squeeze onto your toothbrush.

tow-truck.etymology: tow + truck. Tow comes from Old English togian (to pull, to drag), the same root as tug; truck from Greek trokhos (wheel). Together: the truck that tows a car away.

towel.etymology: From Old French toaille, tracing back to Proto-Germanic thwahlijo, 'a cloth for wiping'. Its cognates across Germanic all relate to washing and wiping. The core feeling: an absorbent cloth you dry off with.

towel-rack.etymology: towel + rack. Rack comes from Middle English rakke, originally 'an upright framework'. Together: the rack you hang towels on.

traffic-cone.etymology: traffic + cone. Traffic comes from Old Italian traffico (commercial dealings, extended to 'the flow of vehicles'); cone from Greek kōnos (pinecone, cone). Together: the cone that directs traffic — bright orange by international convention.

traffic-light.etymology: traffic + light. Traffic comes from Old Italian traffico; light from Old English lēoht. Together: the light that directs traffic — its three-color design was borrowed from railway signals.

traffic-sign.etymology: traffic + sign. Traffic comes from Old Italian traffico (movement to and fro); sign from Latin signum. Together: the sign that directs drivers.

train.etymology: From Old French train (a dragging, a series), from trainer (to drag). So train's core is 'a series of things dragged behind' — the earliest trains were a steam engine dragging one carriage after another.

tram.etymology: From Lowland Scots tram (a beam), originally the little cart that pushed coal along rails in mines. The concept moved up to the street and became today's streetcar, so tram carries the industrial flavor of 'a little car on rails'.

trash-bag.etymology: trash + bag. Trash originally meant 'twig-clippings, refuse', possibly from Old Norse tros (debris); bag from Old Norse baggi (bundle). Together: the bag for trash.

trash-can.etymology: trash + can. Trash possibly comes from Old Norse tros (twig-clippings, refuse); can from Old English canne (container). Together: the can for trash.

tree.etymology: From Old English trēow, tracing back to Proto-Germanic *trewą, meaning 'tree, wood'. One of English's oldest, most basic words — it shares its deepest root with true (real, firm), for the ancients saw the tree as something 'solid and trustworthy'.

tricycle.etymology: tri- (three) + cycle. Tri comes from Greek 'three'; cycle from Greek kyklos (wheel). Literally 'three wheels' — named in parallel with bicycle (two wheels), and just as precise.

truck.etymology: From Greek trokhos (wheel). So truck's roots point straight to 'the wheel' — its core component — before narrowing to the modern sense of 'a large goods vehicle'.

tunnel.etymology: From Old French tonel (a small cask), a diminutive of tonne (a large cask). Originally 'a barrel-shaped thing', it extended to 'a barrel-shaped underground passage' — a tunnel's cross-section really does look like a barrel sliced lengthwise.

turmeric-powder.etymology: turmeric + powder. Turmeric possibly comes from Latin terra merita ('deserving earth'), because its bright yellow resembles a pigment earth. Together: turmeric ground to a yellow powder — the source of curry's signature color.

tv.etymology: Short for television. tele- (far) + -vision (seeing). Tele comes from Greek 'distant'; vision from Latin videre (to see). Together 'the far-off image' — the counterpart to telephone, 'the far-off voice'.

tv-stand.etymology: TV + stand. Stand comes from the verb stand, 'a support that can stand upright'. Together: the stand you set the TV on.

underpass.etymology: under (beneath) + pass. Under comes from Old English under; pass from Old French passer (to pass through). Plainly: the way that passes underneath.

utility-knife.etymology: utility + knife. Utility comes from Latin utilitas (usefulness), from the root uti (to use). Together: a versatile knife that cuts just about anything.

utility-pole.etymology: utility + pole. Utility comes from Latin utilitas (usefulness); pole from Latin palus (stake, post). Together: the pole raised for public utilities — power, phone, and cable all hang on it.

van.etymology: Short for caravan, from Persian kārvān (a caravan) — the great wagons of the traders who moved along the Silk Road. So van hides a piece of Silk Road caravan history, finally shrinking to any boxy transport vehicle.

vanilla-extract.etymology: vanilla + extract. Vanilla comes from Spanish vainilla (a little pod), a diminutive of vaina (pod); extract from Latin extrahere (to draw out). Together: the liquid drawn out of the vanilla pod.

vanity-table.etymology: vanity + table. Vanity comes from Latin vanitas (emptiness), originally 'conceit', later 'a place for grooming yourself' — after all, grooming is about looking good, with a touch of preoccupation with appearance. Together: the table for grooming and dressing up.

vase.etymology: From Latin vas, meaning 'a vessel, a container'. French passed the word to English while keeping its Latin elegance, so vase has carried the refined feel of 'a decorative vessel' from the start.

vegetable-oil.etymology: vegetable + oil. Vegetable comes from Late Latin vegetabilis (living, able to grow); oil from Latin oleum (olive oil). Together it broadly means 'oil from plants', as opposed to animal fat.

vending-machine.etymology: vending + machine. Vend comes from Latin vendere (to sell); machine from Latin machina (device). Together: a machine that sells things — the coin-operated dispenser had prototypes as far back as ancient Rome.

vendor.etymology: From Latin venditor: vendere (to sell) + -tor (agent). So vendor literally means 'one who sells' — a pure core feeling, big or small, as long as they're the seller.

ventilation-fan.etymology: ventilation + fan. Ventilation comes from Latin ventilare (to fan, to let wind through), from the root ventus (wind). Together: the fan that circulates the air.

vinegar.etymology: From Old French vin aigre, literally 'sour wine' (vin wine + aigre sour). So vinegar's roots reveal exactly how it's made — let wine keep fermenting and it turns to vinegar.

wall-art.etymology: wall + art. Wall comes from Old English weall (Latin vallum, rampart); art from Latin ars (skill, craft). Together: art hung on the wall.

wardrobe.etymology: From Old French warderobe: warder (to guard) + robe (garments), literally 'a place that guards your clothes'. So a wardrobe's core feeling is 'a little room where your clothes are kept safe'.

wasabi.etymology: From Japanese 山葵 (wasabi), originally the plant that grows beside Japan's mountain streams. English borrowed the Japanese pronunciation directly, keeping its authentic Japanese-cuisine identity.

wash-basin.etymology: wash + basin. Basin comes from Old French bacin, tracing back to Late Latin baccinum (a shallow bowl). Together: the shallow bowl for washing.

washbasin.etymology: wash + basin written as one word. Wash comes from Old English wæscan; basin from Old French bacin (a shallow bowl). Exactly the same meaning as wash basin, just spelled solid.

water-dispenser.etymology: water + dispenser. Dispense comes from Latin dispensare (to distribute, to weigh out), from the root pendere (to hang, to weigh). Together: the machine that dispenses water.

water-heater.etymology: water + heater. Heater is the verb heat + -er. Both water and heat are basic Old English words (wæter, hǣtu). Plainly: the machine that heats water.

webcam.etymology: web + cam. Web is short for World Wide Web; cam is short for camera. Literally 'a little camera for the web' — a digital product born in the 1990s.

whisk.etymology: From Old Norse visk, meaning 'a little broom, a wisp of twigs'. The earliest whisks were just a bundle of twigs, so whisk's core feeling is still 'a bundle of strands stirred fast'.

white-pepper.etymology: white + pepper. Pepper comes from Sanskrit pippali, traveling the spice roads into Europe. Together: white peppercorns with the outer skin removed — the same plant as black pepper, but milder in flavor.

white-sugar.etymology: white + sugar. Sugar comes from Arabic sukkar and Sanskrit śarkarā. Together: sugar refined all the way to white, as opposed to brown sugar that keeps its molasses.

white-vinegar.etymology: white + vinegar. Vinegar is French vin aigre (sour wine). Together: colorless, clear vinegar fermented from distilled alcohol, as opposed to black or rice vinegar.

whiteboard.etymology: white + board. White comes from Old English hwīt; board from Old English bord (plank). Together: a white board — the office and teaching tool that replaced the blackboard in the late 20th century.

whiteboard-marker.etymology: whiteboard + marker. Marker is mark + -er. Together: the pen for marking on a whiteboard — the wipeable kind.

window.etymology: From Old Norse vindauga, literally 'wind eye' (vindr is wind, auga is eye). The Vikings called the hole in the wall that let in air and light a 'wind eye', and that poetic name carried into English.

wok.etymology: From Cantonese 鑊 (wok6), a Cantonese-cooking word English borrowed directly. It entered the English-speaking world with Chinese cuisine in the 20th century, keeping the core feeling of its original 'big round-bottomed pan' shape.

yellow-mustard.etymology: yellow + mustard. Mustard comes from Latin mustum (new wine) — mustard seeds were once ground into grape juice. Together: a bright yellow mustard, its color coming from added turmeric.
